Your board, in plain language

What it is, how it powers itself, what arrives already built, and the eight wires you attach by hand.

1. What the board actually is

It's a small square of fibreglass — 19.3 × 19.3 mm, about the size of a postage stamp — that drops into a slot in your keyboard.

Its job: read your fingerprint and tell your computer, over Bluetooth, that it's you. It has no battery cable, no USB, no switch. It powers itself from your keyboard's backlight.

Inside that fibreglass are four separate sheets of copper, stacked like pages, with the electrical connections etched into them. That's what "4-layer" means — the wiring runs on four levels so it can all fit in a stamp-sized square.

2. How it powers itself

This is the clever part, and it's why the design is unusual:

Keyboard backlight LEDs→ 3 contacts underneath→ U2 harvester chip→ charges the cell→ U3/U4 steady 3.3 V→ sensor + radio

Your keyboard's backlight is already there, already powered. The board taps a tiny amount of that through contacts on its underside, and U2 (the "charger") turns that trickle into a charge for a small rechargeable cell. U3 and U4 then make the clean, steady 3.3 volts the sensor and radio need.

The whole thing needs about 4 mWh a day — roughly what the backlight gives it in four hours of use, with about 4× to spare.

3. What arrives from JLCPCB, already built

29 components, all soldered on by machine. You don't touch any of these:

Name on boardWhat it isSize
U1The brain and the Bluetooth radio, in one metal-lidded module10.5 × 15.5 mm
U2The harvester — sips power from the backlight and charges the cell3.5 mm square
U3, U4Two voltage regulators, making steady 3.3 V1.0 × 0.8 mm
L1A coil the harvester needs to do its job2.5 × 2.0 mm
C1–C13Twelve capacitors — small energy buffers1.0 × 0.5 mm
R1–R7, ROK, ROVTwelve resistors, mostly setting voltage thresholds1.0 × 0.5 mm

Look at U3 and U4 — one millimetre, with four connections underneath. That is why the board is machine-assembled. Nobody solders those by hand.

4. The eight wires you attach

Everything above arrives done. You add eight wires. Here's where they go — this is the board seen from the top, with the components on it:

The six sensor wires — three each side

SidePadWhat it carries
Left, topJ2-1Power to the sensor (always on, so it can wait for a finger)
Left, middleJ2-2"A finger arrived" — the sensor's way of waking the board up
Left, bottomJ2-3Power to the sensor's own processor (switched off when idle, to save energy)
Right, topJ2-4The sensor talking to the board
Right, middleJ2-5The board talking to the sensor
Right, bottomJ2-6Ground — the common return that every circuit needs

Get the sensor's wire order right before you solder anything. This exact table was wrong earlier in the project — it had been copied from a different sensor model and was reversed end-for-end. Check your sensor's own datasheet against this table, and if they disagree, stop and ask. Swapping power and ground will destroy the sensor instantly.

The two cell wires

Bigger pads, further apart, on the upper left. BT1-1 is +, BT1-2 is −. There's a + and − printed on the board next to them.

5. How to actually solder them

If you've never done this: the pads are bare gold-plated copper circles. You're melting a small amount of solder to join a wire to each circle. The technique that works:

  1. Tin the pad first. Touch the iron to the pad, feed a little solder, remove both. You want a small shiny dome, not a blob.
  2. Tin the wire end. Strip about 2 mm, twist the strands, melt a little solder into them so they hold their shape.
  3. Join them. Hold the tinned wire onto the tinned pad, touch the iron to both for about a second. The two pools merge. Remove the iron and don't move the wire until it dulls — a second or two.
  4. Tug it gently. If it moves, redo it. A joint that looks fine but isn't bonded is the most common failure.

Kit: a fine-tipped iron around 320 °C, thin solder (0.5 mm or less), flux, tweezers, and a magnifier. The pads are 1.2–1.4 mm across — about the size of the tip of a ballpoint pen — so they're comfortable, but you do want to see what you're doing.

The cell pads are the easier pair: bigger, further apart, and only two of them. The sensor's six are the fiddlier job.

6. Do it in this order

  1. Boards arrive from JLCPCB with all 29 parts fitted.
  2. Test before attaching anything. Feed 3.3 V from a bench supply to the test points and check the board behaves. Nothing is at risk yet.
  3. Solder the six sensor wires. Check the pinout twice first.
  4. Fit the board into the 3D-printed housing.
  5. Drop the cell into its pocket above U1 and solder its two wires last.
  6. Slide the module into the keyboard slot. The keyboard's spring-loaded pins press up on the contacts underneath — nothing to solder there.

Why the cell goes last: until it's connected, there's no stored energy anywhere on the board. You can probe, re-solder and make mistakes safely. Once a lithium cell is attached, a slip with a metal tool can short it. Leaving it to the end isn't just convenient — it's the safe order.

One thing is still unresolved, and it matters. The cell needs a small protection circuit, and there isn't room for one on the board. That means buying the cell as a protected assembly — a cell that comes with the protection and its wires already fitted. Do not wire a bare, unprotected lithium cell to this board. It's the one open item that could actually hurt you rather than just waste a board.
